one_liner: RocksDB fork, API-compatible through RocksDB 8.6.7, adding a hash-based memtable and gradual write throttling to beat stock RocksDB.
what_it_does: Speedb is a fork of RocksDB that keeps RocksDB's public headers (include/rocksdb) and API, so an existing RocksDB application relinks against the speedb library instead of rocksdb. It adds engine features, mostly opt-in: a sorted hash memtable (speedb.HashSpdRepFactory), a paired Bloom filter, proactive flushes, a dynamic and global delayed-write controller, non-blocking CompactRange, and an EnableSpeedbFeatures()/SharedOptions helper that turns these on from a RAM budget, a thread count and a delayed-write rate. The last release, 2.8.0 (January 2024), is rebased on RocksDB 8.6.7.
how_it_is_fast: The sorted hash memtable replaces RocksDB's skiplist with a fixed array of hash buckets (MurmurHash of the user key). Each bucket is a short sorted linked list with its own reader-writer lock, so point writes and Gets are bucket probes instead of O(log n) skiplist walks. Each insert also goes onto an atomic, unsorted write list that a background thread cuts into sorted vectors (up to 10K keys each, or whenever a seek arrives). Iterators merge those vectors with a binary heap, so writes keep flowing while a seek waits only for its own cut to be sorted, and a pre-built standby memtable hides the cost of allocating the buckets. Separately, dynamic delayed writes (use_dynamic_delay, on by default) cut the write rate in linear steps according to how far L0 file count, pending compaction bytes or memtable count are past the slowdown trigger. RocksDB instead moves the rate by fixed +25%/-20% steps, and the README's no-stall chart credits this change.
when_to_use: You run RocksDB 7.x to 8.6 and overwrite- or update-heavy workloads with roughly 1KB values are limited by the skiplist memtable; setting memtable_factory to speedb.HashSpdRepFactory is the change the vendor benchmarks (up to +155% overwrite, +68% on a 50% read mix).

Sustained bulk random writes where RocksDB's delayed-write mechanism gives sawtooth throughput and stalls; Speedb's dynamic delay (default on) and a shared WriteController smooth the write rate across column families and across several DBs in one process.
Many DB instances or column families in one process sharing one memory budget: SharedOptions gives them one cache, one WriteBufferManager with proactive flushes, and one write controller.
Filters with high bits-per-key (about 20 and up) where filter memory matters: the paired Bloom filter claims about 30% less memory at the same false-positive rate.
You want to A/B a RocksDB-compatible engine with almost no code change; the docs say you can switch back to RocksDB at any time.
when_not_to_use: You need RocksDB features, fixes or on-disk options added after 8.6.7 (September 2023). Speedb has not rebased since then and has had no commits since March 2024, when Redis acquired the company.

Memory-constrained deployments using the hash memtable. In one Speedb test log (issue #749), malloc stats showed 6040 MB with hash spdb vs 3292 MB with the skiplist. Issue #540 says memtable memory is underestimated, and more so with HashSpdRepFactory. A memory-reduction ticket (#618) is still open.
Workloads dominated by seeks or scans: the claimed gain is only up to 15%, and a seek over freshly written data has to wait for the background thread to sort the pending write list.
Code that relies on Iterator::Refresh() or memtable insert hints: the hash memtable reports IsRefreshIterSupported()=false, and InsertKeyWithHint ignores the hint.
Latency-sensitive point reads through the paired Bloom filter: Speedb's own doc says building and probing it is about 2x slower than RocksDB's default filter, so it saves memory, not time.

integration.form: static lib or shared lib (CMake/make targets speedb and speedb-shared)
integration.dependencies: None required for the core library. Optional: snappy, lz4, zlib, zstd, bzip2 and jemalloc. The CMake option WITH_LIBURING defaults to ON. gflags is needed for db_bench and the tools.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; GCC 7+ or Clang 5+ per INSTALL.md; Visual Studio 2017+ on Windows
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows and iOS per INSTALL.md, with CMake code paths for x86-64, aarch64 (armv8 CRC), ppc64 and s390x. The default build targets the build machine's CPU; use PORTABLE=1 for a portable binary.
integration.thread_safety: Same threading model as the RocksDB code it forks. The hash memtable declares concurrent-insert support, using a reader-writer lock per bucket plus one background sort thread per memtable (SpdbVectorContainer::SortThread).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same include/rocksdb headers and API, and the docs call it fully compatible and reversible. But you link speedb instead of rocksdb, the API stops at RocksDB 8.6.7, the speedups need opt-in options (or EnableSpeedbFeatures), and several defaults differ from RocksDB.

gotchas: Some defaults differ from RocksDB: level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes=false (Speedb's changelog says the flag 'is not working properly with Speedb', issue #786), compaction_readahead_size=0, 8 compaction threads, and use_dynamic_delay=true. A tuned RocksDB config can therefore behave differently.

The docs describe hash-memtable writes as needing no synchronization, but the code takes a per-bucket write lock on every insert. ApproximateMemoryUsage() returns 0, and the bucket vector is allocated outside the arena, so memtable size accounting undercounts.

Bucket count is a fixed cost paid per memtable: the docs cite 1,000,000 buckets (about 8 MB, and creation is slow), while main lowered the default to 400,000 (#854) after the last release. Speedb pre-creates a standby memtable to hide the creation time.
The Speedb write flow (use_spdb_writes) is still marked experimental and uses more memory. How to go back to RocksDB after enabling Speedb-only memtable or filter options is not documented.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Speedb over ToplingDB or PsiTri's RocksDB-API layer when you want the smallest behavioral change from stock RocksDB 8.x (same LSM engine, speedups that are opt-in memtable and filter swaps) and can live with an unmaintained fork. Pick Titan for large values, where its gains come from key-value separation, and ToplingDB if you want a RocksDB fork with larger published speedups and benchmark runs as recent as September 2026.
verified_claims_summary: Speedb's own docs benchmark Speedb with the sorted hash memtable against RocksDB v7.2.2 with its default skiplist, the same RocksDB base as Speedb 2.0/2.1, using db_bench (1B objects, 1KB values, 64MB write buffers, 4 threads, 16 cores, no compression). They report headline 'up to' gains of 155% on 100% overwrite, 68% on a 50% random-read mix and 15% on random seek; per-point values appear only in charts, and no CPU model, compiler or flags are given. The README's no-stall random-write chart (80M objects, 1KB values, 50 threads, 16-core Xeon Platinum 8370C) has no numbers at all.
status_note: Stale: last commit March 2024 and last release 2.8.0 (January 2024, on RocksDB 8.6.7) after Redis acquired Speedb, docs.speedb.io is gone, and 146 issues are still open. It is Apache-2.0 and buildable, but you would have to do every future RocksDB rebase yourself.
